title: Tracheostomy Care
summary: Cleaning and maintaining a tracheostomy stoma and inner cannula.
equipment: Tracheostomy care kit or: sterile NS, hydrogen peroxide (per policy), pipe cleaners/brushes, gauze, sterile gloves, spare tracheostomy tube (same size/type at bedside)
steps: Ensure suction and extra trach tube (same size and one size smaller) are at bedside before starting.
Perform hand hygiene. Don sterile gloves.
Suction the tracheostomy first if secretions are present.
Remove inner cannula if disposable — replace with new one. If reusable — place in hydrogen peroxide (per policy) and clean with brush, rinse with sterile NS, dry.
Clean the stoma site with sterile NS-moistened gauze, moving from inner to outer in a circular motion.
Replace stoma gauze dressing if soiled (split gauze around tube).
Change trach ties if soiled: have assistant hold trach tube in place while one set of ties is removed and replaced. Maintain one finger-width of slack.
Reinsert cleaned/new inner cannula and lock securely.
Assess stoma for granulation tissue, skin breakdown, infection.
Document procedure, secretion color/amount, and site appearance.
nursing_considerations: Never leave the tracheostomy unattended during tie change — accidental decannulation is a medical emergency.
Keep obturator and extra tube taped to head of bed at all times.
Perform care at minimum every 8 hours and whenever soiled.
Avoid over-suctioning — limit to 10 seconds per suction pass.
Inflate cuff appropriately if ventilated — check cuff pressure every 8–12 hours (goal 20–30 cmH2O).

title: Endotracheal Tube (ETT) Management
summary: Monitoring, securing, and maintaining a patient's endotracheal tube during mechanical ventilation.
equipment: Commercial ET tube holder or tape
End-tidal CO2 (EtCO2) monitor or colorimetric CO2 detector
steps: Confirm tube placement: bilateral breath sounds, chest rise, EtCO2, CXR (gold standard).
Document and verify the cm marking at the lip (common adult: 21–23 cm at lip for women, 23–25 cm for men).
Check cuff pressure using a cuff manometer: goal 20–30 cmH2O. Overinflation causes tracheal ischemia; underinflation causes aspiration and air leak.
Assess ET tube security: holder or tape should be intact and snug but not compressing soft tissue or causing pressure injury at lip/mouth corners.
Reposition the tube to the opposite side of the mouth every 24–48 hours (with two nurses) to prevent pressure injury.
Suction as needed: oropharyngeal secretions above the cuff (use Yankauer), and tracheal secretions through inline or open suction catheter.
Inline suction: disconnect ventilator only when necessary. Use closed suction system when available.
Oral care every 4 hours: brush teeth with soft toothbrush, apply CHG oral rinse per VAP bundle, suction secretions.

Assess for complications: mainstem intubation (right shift of unilateral breath sounds), cuff leak (audible gurgling around tube, low tidal volumes on vent), tube obstruction (sudden high peak pressures).
HOB at 30–45° at all times unless contraindicated — reduces aspiration and VAP risk.
Document: tube position (cm at lip), cuff pressure, breath sounds, secretion character, oral care provided.
nursing_considerations: Never pull back or reposition an ETT without a physician/CRNA/RT order — extubation or mainstem intubation risks are high.
VAP (Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia) bundle: HOB 30–45°, daily sedation vacations, spontaneous breathing trials, oral CHG care, avoid unnecessary position changes.
Cuff pressure must be checked every 8–12 hours — do not assume volume-based inflation maintains correct pressure.
Sudden rise in peak airway pressures indicates: kinked tubing, tube obstruction, mucus plug, pneumothorax, or bronchospasm — systematically troubleshoot.
If accidental extubation occurs: maintain airway with jaw thrust/BVM, call STAT, prepare for reintubation.

title: Bag-Valve Mask (BVM) Ventilation
summary: Providing manual positive-pressure ventilation using a bag-valve mask device.
equipment: Bag-valve mask (adult: 1L bag, appropriate mask size)
Oxygen source (connect at 15 L/min for ~100% FiO2 with reservoir)
steps: Assess: unresponsive, agonal breathing, or respiratory arrest — initiate BVM immediately.
Perform hand hygiene. Don gloves and face protection.
Position patient supine. Apply head-tilt chin-lift (or jaw thrust if spinal injury suspected) to open airway.
Insert appropriately sized OPA or NPA to maintain airway patency if patient has no gag reflex.
Connect BVM to oxygen at 15 L/min. Ensure reservoir bag inflates.
Select correct mask size (seal should cover nose and mouth without covering eyes or extending below chin).

One-person technique (E-C clamp): place mask over nose and mouth. Use the 'C' formed by thumb and index finger to hold the mask. Use remaining 3 fingers (the 'E') under the mandible to perform jaw thrust and maintain head tilt.
Two-person technique (preferred): one person maintains mask seal with two-hand E-C clamp; second person squeezes the bag.
Deliver each breath over 1 second — until visible chest rise. Do not over-ventilate.
Rate: for respiratory arrest with pulse — 10–12 breaths/min (1 breath every 5–6 seconds). For cardiac arrest (CPR): 2 breaths after every 30 compressions.
After advanced airway placed: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min) — asynchronous from compressions.
Watch for gastric distension from over-ventilation — increases aspiration risk.
Reassess for signs of ROSC or improvement in breathing effort.
Document initiation, duration, tidal volumes (if monitored), and patient response.
nursing_considerations: Mask seal is the most common point of failure — two-person BVM technique provides significantly better ventilation.
Avoid excessive tidal volumes — use only enough to produce visible chest rise (500–600 mL in adults). Over-ventilation = gastric distension = aspiration.
If chest does not rise: recheck head position, check for airway obstruction, adjust mask seal.
Apply cricoid pressure (Sellick maneuver) if ordered to reduce aspiration risk during BVM ventilation.
BVM is a bridge to definitive airway (intubation, supraglottic airway) — prepare for advanced airway as soon as available team members arrive.

title: Oral Care for Ventilated Patients (VAP Bundle)
summary: Performing evidence-based oral hygiene for intubated patients to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP).
steps: Perform hand hygiene. Don gloves and face protection.
Perform oral care every 4 hours and PRN per VAP bundle protocol.
Suction oropharynx with Yankauer before beginning — clear pooled secretions above the ETT cuff first.
Use soft toothbrush to gently brush teeth, gums, and tongue in circular motions for 1–2 minutes.
Apply or rinse with CHG 0.12% oral solution — do not rinse out (for non-swallowing patients).
Suction oral secretions again with Yankauer.
Apply moisturizing swabs to lips and oral mucosa — ventilated patients develop severe oral dryness.
Assess oral cavity: mucosa color, integrity, presence of ulcers, teeth condition.
Reposition ETT to opposite side of mouth every 24–48 hours as a team (requires 2 nurses).
Ensure HOB remains at 30–45° unless contraindicated (spinal precautions, hypotension).
Document oral assessment, care provided, and ETT position (L/R side and cm mark at lip).
nursing_considerations: VAP bundle components: HOB 30–45°, oral care with CHG every 4 hours, daily sedation vacations, daily spontaneous breathing trials, subglottic suctioning (if specialized ETT available).
VAP is the #1 cause of hospital-acquired infection mortality in ICU patients — oral care compliance directly reduces incidence.
CHG oral care has strong evidence for reducing VAP in cardiac surgery patients; benefit in medical ICU is also supported.
Oral ulcers and pressure injury from ETT are common — reposition tube and use barrier moisture protectants.
Never suction below the ETT cuff without inline suction closed system — open suctioning below the cuff introduces contaminants.
